message.reasoning:
I need to decide on an auction bid for SHORT_LINE.

I have $546 cash and several mortgaged properties. The opponent has $225 and a strong orange and dark blue monopoly. Two players are already bankrupt.

The current bid is $50. I will raise it incrementally to $99 and mortgage immediately. This nets $1 to $49 cash profit. Folding would gift the opponent the railroad cheap.

The opponent can afford to bid up to $225. I will raise the bid to $51.

I am on Water Works. A roll of 2 lands on Marvin Gardens, which is mortgaged and rent-free. A roll of 3 sends me to Jail.

Rolling 7 lands on Short Line, the auctioned property. Rolling 8 would hit Park Place with three houses, charging $1100 in rent. Rolling 9 would hit Boardwalk with three houses, charging $1400. Both are massive rent payments. I have only $546 cash.

I cannot survive Park Place or Boardwalk even with max liquidation. Selling all houses from the light blue monopoly yields $250. That is still too little to cover those rent payments.

Mortgaging States Avenue and Ventnor adds $200 more to liquidation. Total available cash reaches $996. That still falls short of the $1100 rent on Park Place and the $1400 rent on Boardwalk. Buying Short Line at $51 nets $49 profit, pushing total liquid to $1045. Even then, landing on either property would bankrupt me.

The orange monopoly with four houses is equally lethal. St. James Place, Tennessee, and New York charge $750, $875, and $925 in rent respectively. Every dollar saved by the Short Line arbitrage is still needed to survive these smaller hits.

The opponent has matched every bid up to $50, so they may continue raising. Forcing them to $99 nets only $1 profit if they mortgage the property; folding now would give them a $50 profit instead. They already own Reading and Pennsylvania RR, and B&O is mortgaged, so Short Line offers little extra rent value. The mortgage arbitrage remains the stronger reason to keep bidding.
